lead: The air-standard cycle is a clean upper limit, but a real engine burns a fuel-air mixture whose specific heats rise with temperature and whose hot products dissociate. The fuel-air cycle keeps the ideal processes and adds these real properties of the working fluid; it explains why a real engine can never reach the air-standard figure even with perfect hardware. The actual cycle, read from an indicator diagram of a running engine, then adds the losses of the machine: finite burning time, heat loss to the walls, early exhaust opening, pumping and friction. Engineers use the three levels to see where the gap between the textbook efficiency and the measured one comes from.
prereq: You need the Otto cycle and its worked example from ideal air-standard cycles, and the valve events from valve and port timing diagrams.

blocks.text: The fuel-air cycle keeps the air-standard processes (isentropic compression and expansion, instantaneous constant-volume burning in the Otto form, no heat loss, no friction) but uses the real working fluid. Four effects change the result:

items: Variable specific heats. cp and cv of gases rise with temperature, and γ falls. The same heat then raises the temperature less, so the peak temperature and pressure are lower, and the lower γ reduces the work of expansion.

Dissociation. Above about 1600 K some CO₂ and H₂O break back into CO, H₂, O₂ and OH, absorbing heat. Part of it comes back as the gas cools during expansion, but too late in the stroke to give full work. Dissociation cuts the peak temperature most near the chemically correct mixture.
Change in the number of molecules. Burning changes the number of moles; for petrol the products have a few per cent more moles than the reactants, which raises the pressure slightly.
Composition of the charge. The fresh charge mixes with residual burnt gas left from the previous cycle, and its fuel content (the mixture strength) sets how much heat is released.

blocks.text: The result is that the fuel-air cycle efficiency is well below the air-standard value at the same compression ratio; for a chemically correct petrol mixture it is typically about four fifths of it. Values for each compression ratio and mixture strength are read from fuel-air charts.

sections.h3: Effect of mixture strength and compression ratio

blocks.text: The mixture strength is measured by the equivalence ratio φ, the actual fuel-air ratio divided by the chemically correct one (φ = 1 correct, φ > 1 rich, φ < 1 lean).

items: Efficiency rises as the mixture is made leaner: a lean mixture burns cooler, so specific heats stay lower and there is little dissociation. A rich mixture wastes fuel that finds no oxygen.
Power is highest with a slightly rich mixture, about φ = 1.1 to 1.2: all the air is used, and the excess fuel cools the charge.
Raising the compression ratio raises the fuel-air efficiency, as in the air-standard cycle, and the ratio of fuel-air to air-standard efficiency stays roughly the same.

blocks.text: This is why an SI engine is set slightly rich for full power and leaner for cruising economy.

sections.h3: Actual cycle: the losses read from the indicator diagram

blocks.text: An indicator diagram records cylinder pressure against volume in a running engine. Figure 1.8.1 lays it over the ideal Otto cycle; the gap between them is made of these losses:

items: Time loss: burning takes 40° to 60° of crank angle, not zero, so the spark is advanced and part of the pressure rise happens while the piston is still compressing and part after it has started down. The top of the diagram is rounded and lower.
Heat loss to the cylinder walls, head and piston during combustion and expansion lowers the expansion line. Cooling water carries roughly a quarter to a third of the fuel energy away.
Exhaust blowdown loss: the exhaust valve opens before BDC, so the corner at the end of expansion is cut off; some work is lost to cut the pumping work of the exhaust stroke.
Pumping loss: drawing in the charge below atmospheric pressure and pushing out the exhaust above it makes a small negative loop at the bottom of the diagram. It is largest at part throttle.
Incomplete combustion and leakage: some fuel leaves unburnt and some gas leaks past the rings.
Rubbing friction in rings, bearings and the valve train, and the power to drive the pumps, take work after the indicator diagram: they separate indicated from brake work.

blocks.text: With indicated work W<sub>i</sub> (net area of the diagram), brake work W<sub>b</sub> and fuel energy Q<sub>f</sub> per cycle: η<sub>i</sub> = W<sub>i</sub>/Q<sub>f</sub>, η<sub>m</sub> = W<sub>b</sub>/W<sub>i</sub> and η<sub>b</sub> = W<sub>b</sub>/Q<sub>f</sub> = η<sub>i</sub> η<sub>m</sub>. The measurement of these powers is taught in the unit on engine testing and performance.

figure.caption: An SI engine’s indicator diagram (solid) over its ideal Otto cycle (dashed). Finite burning rounds and lowers the top, wall heat loss lowers the expansion line, early exhaust opening cuts the corner at BDC, and the small negative loop at atmospheric pressure is the pumping work. In the second worked example the main loop gave 380 J and the pumping loop 18 J.

spec.aria: Sketch of pressure against volume. A dashed ideal Otto loop with a sharp top; inside it a solid actual loop with a rounded, lower peak, a lower expansion line and a cut-off corner at bottom dead centre. At the bottom a thin shaded pumping loop near atmospheric pressure. Labels mark the spark, time loss, heat loss, exhaust valve opening and the pumping loop.

examples.question: The Otto cycle of the air-standard worked example (r = 8, 1 bar and 300 K, q<sub>in</sub> = 797.5 kJ/kg) reached 1800 K with constant c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Repeat the heat addition with a specific heat that rises with temperature, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.71 + 0.00019 T kJ/kg·K, keeping T₂ = 689.2 K and p₂ = 18.38 bar. Find the new peak temperature and pressure.
steps: Heat added at constant volume: q<sub>in</sub> = ∫c<sub>v</sub> dT = 0.71(T₃ − T₂) + 0.000095(T₃² − T₂²).
Peak pressure at constant volume: p₃ = 18.38 × 1553/689.2 = 41.4 bar.
Compared with constant c<sub>v</sub>: 247 K cooler and 6.6 bar lower at the peak, because the mean c<sub>v</sub> over the heating is 797.5/864 = 0.923, not 0.718 kJ/kg·K.
examples.answer: T₃ = 1553 K and p₃ = 41.4 bar, against 1800 K and 48.0 bar with constant specific heat; the expansion work, and with it the efficiency, falls too.

examples.question: A single-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine of 500 cm³ swept volume runs at 3000 rev/min. Its indicator diagram gives 380 J for the main loop and 18 J for the pumping loop per cycle. A brake test gives 290 J of shaft work per cycle, and it uses 0.0255 g of petrol (calorific value 44 MJ/kg) per cycle. Find the indicated mep, the indicated, mechanical and brake efficiencies, and the friction power.
steps: Net indicated work: W<sub>i</sub> = 380 − 18 = 362 J (the pumping loop is negative work).
Fuel energy per cycle: Q<sub>f</sub> = 0.0255 × 10⁻³ kg × 44 × 10⁶ J/kg = 1122 J.
Cycles per second: 3000/120 = 25. Indicated power 362 × 25 = 9.05 kW; brake power 290 × 25 = 7.25 kW; friction power 9.05 − 7.25 = 1.80 kW.
Against the air-standard 56.5 % at r = 8, the engine reaches 32.3/56.5 = 0.57 of the ideal in indicated terms.
examples.answer: imep 7.24 bar; η<sub>i</sub> 32.3 %, η<sub>m</sub> 80.1 %, η<sub>b</sub> 25.8 %; friction power 1.80 kW.

traps: The fuel-air cycle is still ideal: it has no friction, no heat loss and no pumping. Those belong to the actual cycle.
Variable specific heat lowers the peak temperature for the same heat input; it does not raise it. The specific heat goes up, so ΔT = q/c<sub>v</sub> goes down.
Maximum power and maximum efficiency do not come at the same mixture: power slightly rich, efficiency lean.
The pumping loop is subtracted from the main loop to get net indicated work, not added.

Indicated efficiency is before friction; brake efficiency is η<sub>i</sub> × η<sub>m</sub>. Percentage points are not per cent: 56.5 % to 32.3 % is a fall of 24.2 points, or 43 per cent of the ideal value.

quiz.q: List three effects a fuel-air cycle includes that an air-standard cycle leaves out.
quiz.a: Specific heats that vary with temperature, dissociation of the products, and the change in the number of molecules on burning (also the real charge composition with residual gas).

quiz.q: Name four losses that separate the actual cycle from the fuel-air cycle.
quiz.a: Time loss of finite burning, heat loss to the walls, exhaust blowdown loss, pumping loss (also leakage, incomplete combustion and friction).

quiz.q: Why is the fuel-air efficiency lower than the air-standard efficiency at the same r?
quiz.a: The specific heats rise with temperature and dissociation absorbs heat at the peak, so the same fuel energy gives a lower peak temperature and pressure; the lower γ also reduces the expansion work.

quiz.q: Why is the spark advanced before TDC?
quiz.a: Burning takes 40° to 60° of crank angle. Starting it early centres the pressure rise near TDC and makes the time loss as small as possible.

quiz.q: An engine has an indicated efficiency of 36 % and a mechanical efficiency of 85 %. Find its brake efficiency.
A cylinder of 400 cm³ swept volume gives 320 J in its main loop and 14 J in its pumping loop. Find the net indicated work and the imep.
A student says: “Rich mixtures give more power, so they must give more efficiency too.” Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Power is highest slightly rich (φ about 1.1 to 1.2) because all the air is used. Efficiency is highest lean, because the cooler burning keeps specific heats low and avoids dissociation, and no fuel leaves unburnt. A rich mixture gives more power per cycle but less work per unit of fuel.

beyond: Engine developers fit thermodynamic models with variable properties and chemical equilibrium to measured cylinder-pressure traces, and split the losses exactly as in this chapter. Heat-release analysis of the pressure trace tells how fast the fuel burned in each cycle. Search for heat release analysis, Wiebe function and fuel-air cycle charts.
